title: enrich with customers
statement:
Python Engineer · pandas

Build enrich_with_customers

Left-join customer name and tier onto orders, safely.

- customers has customer_id, name, tier.

- Pass validate="many_to_one" so a duplicated customer_id RAISES instead of

silently multiplying your rows. That single keyword is the whole point of this

exercise.

- Orders whose customer is unknown are kept, with name = "unknown" and

tier = "none".

- Row count and order are unchanged from orders.

- Raise ValueError if customers has duplicate ids (catch pandas' MergeError and

re-raise as ValueError, so callers don't have to know you used pandas).

Work through this step

  1. Read the contract and identify its boundary cases.
  2. Run the demonstration to explore the concept.
  3. Edit the module file; focus on this step’s function or class.
  4. Run required checks, then explain one design decision in Notes.
Hint

Start with the smallest example in the contract. Read the named failing test; separate the normal behavior from validation and edge cases. Related helpers share this module workspace.

Module concepts & examples

24 — pandas

pandas is a query engine with a Python API. The skill isn't memorising methods — it's

learning to express a whole transformation as vectorised operations over columns

instead of a loop over rows.

This module targets pandas 3.0, which changed two defaults that most tutorials on the

internet predate. Read §2 before anything else.

In plain English

pandas is a spreadsheet you drive with code. A DataFrame is a table — columns with names,

rows of data — and you transform it with operations on whole columns instead of clicking

cells.

The thing that makes it different from a spreadsheet is the index: every row has a

label, and when you combine two tables pandas lines them up *by label*, not by position.

That's powerful and it's the source of the classic confusion — combining two things whose

labels don't match gives you a table full of blanks rather than an error.

The other habit worth building early is vectorised thinking, same as NumPy. Writing a

loop over rows is the natural instinct and it is roughly 75× slower than doing the whole

column at once — and for a conditional, over 1000× slower. The lesson measures both.

One note on version: this course runs on pandas 3.0, which changed a long-standing

behaviour. Most tutorials online predate it. In particular, df[mask]["col"] = value now

silently does *nothing* (it writes to a temporary copy). The correct form is

df.loc[mask, "col"] = value. Worth reading section 2 before you copy anything off the

internet.

Watch out for: merging two tables when the right-hand one has duplicate keys — you

quietly get *more rows than you started with*. Passing validate="many_to_one" turns that

silent disaster into an immediate error.

1. Series and DataFrame

- Series: a typed 1-D array (NumPy or Arrow underneath) plus an index.

- DataFrame: an ordered dict of Series sharing one index.

The index is the thing that makes pandas different from a spreadsheet: it aligns data

automatically in every binary operation.

a = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], index=["x", "y", "z"])
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=["y", "z"])
a + b        # x NaN, y 12, z 23  — aligned by LABEL, not position

That alignment is a feature and a trap: a botched index silently produces NaNs rather than

an error. .reset_index(drop=True) when you don't want it.

2. What changed in pandas 3.0

Copy-on-Write is now the only behaviour. Every operation behaves as if it returned a

copy; a write never propagates to a parent object. This kills SettingWithCopyWarning and

the entire class of "did that assignment land?" bugs.

The practical consequence — chained assignment silently does nothing:

df[df["amount"] > 100]["flagged"] = True    # NO-OP. Writes to a temporary.
df.loc[df["amount"] > 100, "flagged"] = True   # correct

Also: inplace=True no longer avoids a copy. It has no performance benefit and hurts

readability — stop using it and chain instead.

Strings default to a real str dtype, not object. Columns of text are now

Arrow-backed: less memory, much faster string operations, and NaN in a string column is

NA rather than a float.

3. Selecting

df["col"]                 # a Series
df[["a", "b"]]            # a DataFrame
df.loc[rows, cols]        # LABEL based, end-INCLUSIVE
df.iloc[rows, cols]       # POSITION based, end-exclusive
df.at[label, "col"]       # single scalar, fast
df.query("amount > 100 and status == 'ok'")

Boolean masks are the workhorse:

df[(df["amount"] > 100) & (df["status"] == "ok")]      # & | ~ , and MIND THE PARENTHESES
df[df["status"].isin(["ok", "pending"])]
df[df["email"].str.contains("@example", na=False)]
df[df["amount"].between(10, 100)]

and/or raise on Series — use &/|, and parenthesise because they bind tighter than

comparison.

4. dtypes

dtypeUse
int64 / float64numbers; int64 cannot hold NA
Int64 (capital I)nullable integer — an int column with missing values
strtext (Arrow-backed in 3.0)
categorylow-cardinality labels — big memory and groupby wins
datetime64[ns, tz]timestamps; keep them tz-aware (module 19)
bool / booleannon-nullable / nullable

df.dtypes, df.info(memory_usage="deep"), df.astype({"id": "Int64"}),

pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce"), pd.to_datetime(s, format=..., utc=True).

Always pass format= to to_datetime on a known format — it's an order of magnitude

faster and it stops pandas guessing differently on different chunks.

5. Missing data

NaN (float), NaT (datetime), pd.NA (the nullable ones). All are "missing", and none

compare equal to themselves.

df.isna().sum()                 # missing per column — the first thing to run on new data
df.dropna(subset=["email"])
df["amount"].fillna(0)
df["amount"].ffill()            # careful: propagates stale values forward

6. groupby: split → apply → combine

df.groupby("dept")["salary"].mean()
df.groupby(["dept", "level"]).agg(
    headcount=("id", "size"),
    total_pay=("salary", "sum"),
    top_pay=("salary", "max"),
)                                        # named aggregation: flat, readable columns
df.groupby("dept")["salary"].transform("mean")   # broadcast BACK to the original rows
df.groupby("dept").filter(lambda g: len(g) > 5)

Know the difference:

- agg → one row per group.

- transform → same shape as the input (for "salary minus department mean").

- apply → arbitrary, and slow: it runs Python per group. Last resort.

observed=True for categorical keys (otherwise you get the full cartesian product),

dropna=False to keep NA keys, as_index=False to get a flat frame back.

7. Joining

pd.merge(orders, customers, on="customer_id", how="left",
         validate="many_to_one", indicator=True)
pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True)      # stack rows
df.join(other)                                 # index-based, convenience wrapper

Always pass validate=. "many_to_one", "one_to_one" etc. turn a silent row

explosion — the classic "why do I have 4 million rows now?" — into an immediate error.

indicator=True adds a _merge column so you can count what didn't match.

8. Reshaping and time series

df.pivot_table(index="region", columns="month", values="sales", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0)
df.melt(id_vars="id", var_name="metric", value_name="value")     # wide -> long
df.set_index("ts").resample("1D").sum()                          # time bucketing
df["amount"].rolling(7).mean()                                    # rolling window
df.sort_values("ts").groupby("user")["amount"].cumsum()

9. Performance

- Never iterrows / itertuples / apply(axis=1) in a hot path. They're a Python

loop with extra allocation. Vectorise, or use np.where/np.select for conditionals.

- category dtype for repeated strings: often 10–100× less memory and much faster groupby.

- Read only what you need: usecols=, dtype=, chunksize= in read_csv.

- Parquet over CSV for anything you write yourself — typed, columnar, compressed.

- dtype_backend="pyarrow" for lower memory and faster strings.

- If your data doesn't fit or pandas is the bottleneck: polars (faster, lazy, saner

API) or DuckDB (SQL over your DataFrames). Both interop through Arrow at zero copy.

10. Style: chain, don't mutate

result = (
    orders
    .loc[lambda d: d["status"].eq("complete")]
    .assign(month=lambda d: d["ts"].dt.to_period("M"))
    .groupby("month", as_index=False)
    .agg(revenue=("amount", "sum"))
    .sort_values("month")
)

Each step is a pure transformation, the whole thing reads top to bottom, and there are no

half-mutated intermediates named df2, df_clean, df_final_v2.

Exercises

exercises_24.py, then pytest 24_pandas.

Further reading

- pandas user guide (optional reading: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/) — "Copy-on-Write" and "group by" especially

- Effective pandas (optional reading: https://github.com/mattharrison) (Harrison) for the chaining style

- polars (optional reading: https://docs.pola.rs/) when pandas stops being enough

Required check source
import time

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest

from courselib import impl

m = impl("24")

RAW = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "order_id": ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6", "2", "7"],
        "customer_id": ["10", "10", "20", "20", "30", "oops", "10", "30"],
        "ts": [
            "2026-01-05 10:00:00",
            "2026-01-20 11:00:00",
            "2026-02-03 09:30:00",
            "2026-02-14 18:45:00",
            "2026-03-01 00:00:00",
            "2026-03-02 00:00:00",
            "2026-01-20 11:00:00",
            "not a date",
        ],
        "amount": ["100.0", "50.5", "200", "-5", "abc", "75", "50.5", "10"],
        "status": ["complete", "complete", "complete", "complete", "complete", "weird", "complete", "pending"],
        "region": [" North ", "north", "SOUTH", "south", "north", "south", "north", "south"],
    }
)


@pytest.fixture
def clean():
    return m.clean_orders(RAW)


class TestCleanOrders:
    def test_drops_unusable_rows(self, clean):
        # order 4 (negative), 5 (bad amount), 7 (bad date), duplicate 2 -> 4 rows left
        assert list(clean["order_id"]) == [1, 2, 3, 6]

    def test_dtypes(self, clean):
        assert clean["order_id"].dtype == "Int64"
        assert clean["customer_id"].dtype == "Int64"
        assert clean["amount"].dtype == "float64"
        assert isinstance(clean["ts"].dtype, pd.DatetimeTZDtype)
        assert str(clean["status"].dtype) == "category"

    def test_timestamps_are_utc(self, clean):
        assert str(clean["ts"].dt.tz) == "UTC"

    def test_region_normalised(self, clean):
        assert set(clean["region"]) <= {"north", "south"}
        assert clean.loc[0, "region"] == "north"

    def test_unknown_status_becomes_na(self, clean):
        assert list(clean["status"].cat.categories) == ["complete", "pending", "cancelled"]
        assert clean.loc[clean["order_id"] == 6, "status"].isna().all()

    def test_bad_customer_id_becomes_na_but_keeps_the_row(self, clean):
        assert clean.loc[clean["order_id"] == 6, "customer_id"].isna().all()

    def test_duplicate_order_id_keeps_the_first(self, clean):
        assert (clean["order_id"] == 2).sum() == 1

    def test_index_is_reset(self, clean):
        assert list(clean.index) == list(range(len(clean)))

    def test_columns_preserved(self, clean):
        assert list(clean.columns) == list(RAW.columns)

    def test_input_is_not_modified(self):
        before = RAW.copy()
        m.clean_orders(RAW)
        pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(RAW, before)

    def test_all_bad_input(self):
        bad = RAW.assign(amount="junk")
        assert len(m.clean_orders(bad)) == 0


class TestRevenueByMonth:
    def test_totals(self, clean):
        got = m.revenue_by_month(clean)
        assert list(got["month"]) == ["2026-01", "2026-02"]
        assert got.loc[0, "revenue"] == pytest.approx(150.5)
        assert got.loc[1, "revenue"] == pytest.approx(200.0)

    def test_counts(self, clean):
        assert list(m.revenue_by_month(clean)["orders"]) == [2, 1]

    def test_columns(self, clean):
        assert list(m.revenue_by_month(clean).columns) == ["month", "revenue", "orders"]

    def test_sorted_and_reset(self, clean):
        got = m.revenue_by_month(clean)
        assert list(got["month"]) == sorted(got["month"])
        assert list(got.index) == list(range(len(got)))

    def test_ignores_non_complete(self, clean):
        # order 6 has an NA status and must not be counted
        assert m.revenue_by_month(clean)["orders"].sum() == 3

    def test_empty_input(self, clean):
        got = m.revenue_by_month(clean.iloc[0:0])
        assert list(got.columns) == ["month", "revenue", "orders"]
        assert len(got) == 0


class TestTopCustomers:
    def test_ranking(self, clean):
        got = m.top_customers(clean, n=2)
        assert list(got["customer_id"]) == [20, 10]
        assert got.loc[0, "total"] == pytest.approx(200.0)

    def test_columns(self, clean):
        assert list(m.top_customers(clean).columns) == ["customer_id", "total", "orders", "avg"]

    def test_average(self, clean):
        got = m.top_customers(clean)
        row = got.loc[got["customer_id"] == 10].iloc[0]
        assert row["avg"] == pytest.approx(75.25)

    def test_respects_n(self, clean):
        assert len(m.top_customers(clean, n=1)) == 1

    def test_n_zero(self, clean):
        got = m.top_customers(clean, n=0)
        assert len(got) == 0
        assert list(got.columns) == ["customer_id", "total", "orders", "avg"]

    def test_index_reset(self, clean):
        assert list(m.top_customers(clean).index) == list(range(len(m.top_customers(clean))))


CUSTOMERS = pd.DataFrame(
    {"customer_id": [10, 20], "name": ["ada", "bob"], "tier": ["gold", "silver"]}
)


class TestEnrichWithCustomers:
    def test_adds_columns(self, clean):
        got = m.enrich_with_customers(clean, CUSTOMERS)
        assert {"name", "tier"} <= set(got.columns)

    def test_row_count_is_unchanged(self, clean):
        assert len(m.enrich_with_customers(clean, CUSTOMERS)) == len(clean)

    def test_matches(self, clean):
        got = m.enrich_with_customers(clean, CUSTOMERS)
        assert got.loc[got["customer_id"] == 10, "name"].eq("ada").all()

    def test_unknown_customers_get_placeholders(self, clean):
        got = m.enrich_with_customers(clean, CUSTOMERS)
        unknown = got.loc[got["customer_id"].isna()]
        assert unknown["name"].eq("unknown").all()
        assert unknown["tier"].eq("none").all()

    def test_duplicate_customers_raise_valueerror(self, clean):
        duplicated = pd.concat([CUSTOMERS, CUSTOMERS], ignore_index=True)
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            m.enrich_with_customers(clean, duplicated)

    def test_does_not_leak_pandas_exceptions(self, clean):
        duplicated = pd.concat([CUSTOMERS, CUSTOMERS], ignore_index=True)
        try:
            m.enrich_with_customers(clean, duplicated)
        except Exception as exc:
            assert not isinstance(exc, pd.errors.MergeError)

    def test_order_preserved(self, clean):
        got = m.enrich_with_customers(clean, CUSTOMERS)
        assert list(got["order_id"]) == list(clean["order_id"])


class TestAddRunningTotal:
    def test_adds_the_column(self, clean):
        assert "running_total" in m.add_running_total(clean).columns

    def test_cumulative_per_customer(self, clean):
        got = m.add_running_total(clean).set_index("order_id")["running_total"]
        assert got[1] == pytest.approx(100.0)
        assert got[2] == pytest.approx(150.5)  # same customer, later
        assert got[3] == pytest.approx(200.0)  # a different customer starts again

    def test_row_order_is_preserved(self, clean):
        got = m.add_running_total(clean)
        assert list(got["order_id"]) == list(clean["order_id"])

    def test_input_not_modified(self, clean):
        before = clean.copy()
        m.add_running_total(clean)
        pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(clean, before)

    @pytest.mark.benchmark
    def test_scales(self):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
        n = 300_000
        big = pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "order_id": range(n),
                "customer_id": rng.integers(0, 1000, n),
                "amount": rng.random(n),
                "ts": pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=n, freq="1min", tz="UTC"),
                "status": "complete",
                "region": "north",
            }
        )
        start = time.perf_counter()
        m.add_running_total(big)
        assert time.perf_counter() - start < 3.0  # a row loop takes minutes


class TestPivotRegionMonth:
    def test_shape_and_values(self, clean):
        got = m.pivot_region_month(clean)
        assert list(got.index) == ["north", "south"]
        assert list(got.columns) == ["2026-01", "2026-02"]
        assert got.loc["north", "2026-01"] == pytest.approx(150.5)

    def test_missing_combinations_are_zero(self, clean):
        assert m.pivot_region_month(clean).loc["north", "2026-02"] == 0.0

    def test_columns_axis_has_no_name(self, clean):
        assert m.pivot_region_month(clean).columns.name is None

    def test_sorted(self, clean):
        got = m.pivot_region_month(clean)
        assert list(got.index) == sorted(got.index)
        assert list(got.columns) == sorted(got.columns)


class TestFlagAnomalies:
    @pytest.fixture
    def frame(self):
        return pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "order_id": range(1, 8),
                "customer_id": [1] * 7,
                "amount": [10.0, 12.0, 11.0, 9.0, 500.0, 20.0, 21.0],
                "region": ["north"] * 5 + ["south"] * 2,
                "status": "complete",
                "ts": pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=7, tz="UTC"),
            }
        )

    def test_adds_columns(self, frame):
        got = m.flag_anomalies(frame)
        assert {"region_mean", "is_anomaly"} <= set(got.columns)

    def test_flags_the_outlier(self, frame):
        got = m.flag_anomalies(frame, n_std=1.0)
        assert got.loc[got["amount"] == 500.0, "is_anomaly"].all()

    def test_normal_rows_are_not_flagged(self, frame):
        got = m.flag_anomalies(frame, n_std=1.0)
        assert not got.loc[got["amount"] == 10.0, "is_anomaly"].any()

    def test_region_mean_is_per_region(self, frame):
        got = m.flag_anomalies(frame)
        north = got.loc[got["region"] == "north", "region_mean"].unique()
        south = got.loc[got["region"] == "south", "region_mean"].unique()
        assert len(north) == 1 and len(south) == 1
        assert north[0] != south[0]

    def test_region_mean_is_broadcast_not_aggregated(self, frame):
        assert len(m.flag_anomalies(frame)) == len(frame)

    def test_single_row_region_is_never_an_anomaly(self):
        frame = pd.DataFrame({"amount": [10.0, 999.0], "region": ["a", "b"]})
        got = m.flag_anomalies(frame)
        assert not got["is_anomaly"].any()

    def test_is_anomaly_is_boolean(self, frame):
        assert m.flag_anomalies(frame)["is_anomaly"].dtype == bool

    def test_input_not_modified(self, frame):
        before = frame.copy()
        m.flag_anomalies(frame)
        pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(frame, before)

    def test_row_order_preserved(self, frame):
        assert list(m.flag_anomalies(frame)["order_id"]) == list(frame["order_id"])

"""Module 24 exercises.  pytest 24_pandas

Rules for this module:
- No `iterrows`, `itertuples` or `apply(axis=1)`. Two tests time large frames and will
  fail a row loop even when it returns the right answer.
- Never mutate an input frame. Under pandas 3.0's copy-on-write you mostly can't by
  accident — but you can still do it deliberately, and the tests check.
- Prefer the chaining style: `.loc[lambda d: ...]`, `.assign(...)`, `.pipe(...)`.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import pandas as pd

# The raw shape the exercises receive: everything is text, some of it is junk.
RAW_COLUMNS = ["order_id", "customer_id", "ts", "amount", "status", "region"]


def clean_orders(raw: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Turn a frame of strings into a typed, validated one.

    Input columns are all text: order_id, customer_id, ts, amount, status, region.

    Output requirements:
    - `order_id`, `customer_id` -> `Int64` (nullable — junk becomes NA, it does not raise)
    - `amount` -> `float64`, via `pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce")`
    - `ts` -> `datetime64[ns, UTC]`, parsed with an explicit `format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"`
      and `utc=True`; unparsable values become NaT
    - `status` -> `category` with exactly the categories
      ["complete", "pending", "cancelled"]; any other value becomes NA. Note: you must
      NA-out the unknown values *before* casting — building a Categorical from values
      outside its own categories is deprecated and raises a Pandas4Warning.
    - `region` -> stripped and lowercased text
    - Rows with NA in `order_id`, `ts` or `amount` are DROPPED (they're unusable)
    - Rows with a negative `amount` are dropped
    - Duplicate `order_id` keeps the FIRST occurrence
    - The index is reset to 0..n-1
    - Column order is preserved

    The input frame must come back unmodified.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def revenue_by_month(orders: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Monthly revenue over completed orders only.

    Returns a frame with columns `["month", "revenue", "orders"]`:
    - `month` is a string "YYYY-MM" (use `.dt.strftime`, not `to_period` — that drops
      the timezone and warns)
    - `revenue` is the summed `amount` as float
    - `orders` is the row count as int
    - sorted by month ascending, index reset
    - months with no completed orders simply don't appear
    - an empty input gives an empty frame WITH those three columns and the right dtypes
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def top_customers(orders: pd.DataFrame, n: int = 3) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The n biggest customers by total completed spend.

    Returns `["customer_id", "total", "orders", "avg"]`:
    - `total` summed amount, `orders` the count, `avg` = total / orders rounded to 2dp
    - sorted by total descending, ties broken by customer_id ascending
    - at most n rows; `n <= 0` gives an empty frame with those columns
    - index reset

    One `groupby(...).agg(...)` with named aggregation, then sort and head. No loop.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def enrich_with_customers(orders: pd.DataFrame, customers: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Left-join customer `name` and `tier` onto orders, safely.

    - `customers` has `customer_id`, `name`, `tier`.
    - Pass `validate="many_to_one"` so a duplicated customer_id RAISES instead of
      silently multiplying your rows. That single keyword is the whole point of this
      exercise.
    - Orders whose customer is unknown are kept, with `name` = "unknown" and
      `tier` = "none".
    - Row count and order are unchanged from `orders`.
    - Raise `ValueError` if `customers` has duplicate ids (catch pandas' MergeError and
      re-raise as ValueError, so callers don't have to know you used pandas).
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def add_running_total(orders: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Add a per-customer running total of `amount`, ordered by time.

    Returns a copy with one extra column `running_total` (float):
    - within each `customer_id`, the cumulative sum of `amount` ordered by `ts`
    - the ORIGINAL row order is preserved — sort, compute, then restore
    - the input is not modified

    `groupby(...)["amount"].cumsum()` on a time-sorted frame does it. The trap is
    returning the rows in sorted order instead of the original order; the tests check.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def pivot_region_month(orders: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Revenue by region (rows) and month (columns), completed orders only.

    - index: `region`, sorted ascending
    - columns: "YYYY-MM" strings, sorted ascending
    - values: summed amount, missing combinations filled with 0.0
    - the columns index has no name (call `.rename_axis(columns=None)`) — pandas leaves
      "month" there otherwise and it breaks frame comparisons
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def flag_anomalies(orders: pd.DataFrame, n_std: float = 2.0) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Flag orders far above their own region's average.

    Returns a copy with two extra columns:
    - `region_mean`: the mean `amount` of that row's region (`transform`, not `agg` —
      you need it broadcast back to every row)
    - `is_anomaly`: True when `amount > region_mean + n_std * region_std`, where
      region_std is the SAMPLE std (ddof=1) of that region

    - A region with fewer than 2 rows has an NA std; those rows are never anomalies.
    - Row order and the input frame are untouched.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError
